The total treasury marketable securities outstanding are owned by two players.  The Fed and the private sector.  Let's clown what's outstanding as 2's and 30's only. 

Total outstanding is 100 units of which 70 units is 2's and 30
Units is 30.  The Wam is (2*70+30*30)/100=10.4 years

Let's say the Fed owns 20% of the total. And is 50/50 that means they hold 16 years of WAM   

The other 80% has to be shorter WAM than 10.4. Turns out is (10.4*100-16*20)/80=9 years 

Ignoring the treasury for the moment.  In order for the Fed wam to go to 10.4 fron 16 they would need to sell 20% of their 30's and buy 20% more twos and they would have to have the private sector take those on such that the private sector WAM would rise.   That rise from 9 to 10.4 would force more risk on the private sector and tighten. 

However the Fed doesn't actually sell it lets its holdings mature and buys new 2's and 30's from the treasury and maintains its 16 WAM.  The treasury can maintain its 10.4 Wam by issuing 9 Wam to the private sector.  IF the Fed unilaterally stopped buying as much 30's such that their wam would fall toward 10.4 over time UNLESS the treasury increased what it sold to the private sector the impact of the Fed change would have no private sector impact and no tightening.  However the Fed's action would impact the total wam issued by treasury downward from 10.4 toward 9.  The treasury would have to decide if that's desirable or not. The Fed can do whatever it wants but ONLY if the treasury adjusts to those changes and issues more 30'z to the private sector (so as to maintain their overall wam) will there be a tightening impact of the Fed shift

"Open weight absolutely matters in the ecosystem. The world cannot just be controlled by proprietary APIs, where open weight, open development and research of these models are blocked or banned."

"Control matters a lot over the last few years, and then cost just started to matter over the last few months... It's about controlling the system performance against what they're paying for."

"For a voice agent company, they want to control their own model so that it can make sure the model actually responds by the required time... Leading indicators do not support expectations of a Fed hike this year.

The US policy leading indicator has rolled over since the beginning of the year, when it was pointing to significant easing. Even so, it remains far from the sub-35 threshold associated with Fed hikes. Real yields have also caught up with that earlier move.

Inflation signals are beginning to turn as well. Our diffusion index for global inflation-leading inputs is now rolling over, an early indication that the global inflation impulse may have peaked. The timing further weakens the case. A single 25bp hike only months before the midterms would offer the Fed limited policy benefit relative to its potential costs.

Growth leading indicators continue to improve, while inflation risks are beginning to ease. That combination keeps the cyclical backdrop risk-on and leaves little support for a Fed hike.

Imagine waking up in 2035.

You pick up your phone. It contains fractal graphene.

You get into your EV. Fractal graphene.

The tires, battery components, lubricants and lightweight composites? Fractal graphene.

The airplane you board. The data center powering AI. Wind turbines. Medical devices. Concrete. Coatings. Packaging. Water filtration. Sporting goods. Electronics. Aerospace. Defense.

Fractal graphene is everywhere.

Not because companies wanted “graphene.”

Because they wanted products that are lighter, stronger, more conductive, more durable and more sustainable.

If HydroGraph’s production process continues to prove scalable, cost-effective and consistent, the opportunity is not about replacing one material in one industry.

I am not saying this future is guaranteed.

I am saying that if fractal graphene becomes a standard performance additive, today’s valuation could one day look astonishingly small.

Sometimes the biggest winners are not the companies selling the finished product.

They are the ones supplying the material inside millions—or even billions—of products.

TL;DR

- The bottleneck for AI is no longer money—it’s power. Capital is abundant, but electricity, transformers, GPUs, cooling, networking and data centres are the scarce resources limiting AI growth. 

- Energy and AI can both be broken into four layers: Make, Move, Store, Sell. This framework helps identify where value will accrue across the stack. 

- For electricity, these correspond to generating power, transmitting it, storing it (batteries/thermal storage), and selling it through utilities and power markets. 

- For AI, they correspond to creating models and chips, networking and interconnects, memory and context storage, and finally applications and APIs that sell intelligence. 

-We are at an inflection point because AI demand has exploded, energy technologies (especially solar and batteries) have become economically viable, governments now view AI and energy as strategic priorities, and a new generation of founders has emerged to build hard-tech companies. 

- The biggest long-term winners will be systems companies that vertically integrate hardware, software, energy and operations rather than pure software businesses. 

- Today’s infrastructure bottlenecks - GPUs, transformers, cooling, networking and power equipment - are tomorrow’s platforms. The biggest companies will emerge by solving these constraints, not simply exploiting them temporarily. 

- Compute factories (next-generation AI data centres) are becoming the “refineries” of the AI era, manufacturing intelligence by integrating power, cooling, networking, chips and software into one system. 

- AI is accelerating an enormous buildout across energy infrastructure, batteries, compute markets and frontier power technologies (SMRs, geothermal, fusion, etc.), compressing decades of learning into just a few years.

- The core investment thesis is simple: intelligence is humanity’s highest-return asset, so the biggest opportunities lie in companies that lower the cost of producing intelligence - or the energy required to create it.
